screens.title: Understanding Windows Privilege Escalation
screens.narratorSegment: When you first gain access to a Windows system, you'll often find yourself operating with low-level user privileges. This means you can't install software, modify critical system files, or access sensitive data. The primary goal of Windows privilege escalation is to elevate these limited privileges, typically aiming for NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM or a local administrator account. Think of NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM as the Windows equivalent of 'root' on a Linux system – it grants ultimate control. Windows environments present a unique set of challenges and opportunities compared to Linux, largely due to its distinct architecture, service management, and security model. For instance, Windows relies heavily on the registry for configuration and has a different approach to user and group permissions. Understanding these fundamental differences is absolutely key to successfully identifying and exploiting vulnerabilities. Without elevated privileges, your ability to further compromise a system or achieve your objectives is severely limited, making this a crucial phase in any penetration test. Understanding Windows Privilege Escalation means privilege escalation aims to gain higher access on windows, moving from a low-privileged user to full system control.. In practical terms, elevating access from low-level user to system.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Core Concept

Understanding Windows Privilege Escalation

Elevating access from low-level user to SYSTEM.

Why Privilege Escalation?

  • Initial access often yields low-level user privileges.
  • Higher privileges (Administrator, SYSTEM) are needed for critical actions.
  • Enables full system control, data access, and persistence.
  • Crucial for achieving penetration testing objectives.

Windows vs. Linux PE

  • Distinct Architecture: Windows has unique service management and security models.
  • Registry Focus: Windows heavily relies on the registry for configuration.
  • Permission Models: Different approaches to user and group permissions.
  • Exploitation Vectors: Unique vulnerabilities like service misconfigurations and specific policies.
Privilege Hierarchy
NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM
Local Administrator
Standard User
Key Takeaway

Privilege escalation aims to gain higher access on Windows, moving from a low-privileged user to full system control.

screens.title: Unquoted Service Paths
screens.narratorSegment: One of the most common and often easily exploitable vulnerabilities on Windows involves service misconfigurations, specifically unquoted service paths. Windows services are programs that run in the background, often with elevated privileges like LocalSystem. When a service's executable path contains spaces, such as 'C:\Program Files\My Application\service. exe', but isn't enclosed in quotation marks, Windows can misinterpret the path. Instead of executing the full path, the operating system might sequentially try to execute each component of the path before the next space. For example, it might first attempt to run 'C:\Program. exe', then 'C:\Program Files\My. exe', and so on. If a low-privileged user can write to any of these intermediate paths, they can place a malicious executable there. When the legitimate service starts or restarts, Windows will inadvertently execute the attacker's payload with the service's high privileges. This is a powerful technique because it leverages a fundamental parsing error in how Windows handles file paths. Identifying these services is a critical first step in exploiting this vulnerability. Unquoted Service Paths means unquoted service paths allow windows to execute malicious code placed in intermediate path segments with elevated service privileges.. In practical terms, exploiting windows' path interpretation for privilege escalation.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5›Chapter 5.3›Unquoted Service Paths
Vulnerability Deep Dive

Unquoted Service Paths

Exploiting Windows' path interpretation for privilege escalation.

How it Works

  • Service path contains spaces (e.g., C:\Program Files\App\service.exe).
  • Path is not enclosed in double quotes.
  • Windows attempts to execute C:\Program.exe first.
  • If C:\Program.exe exists and is writable by a low-priv user, it runs with service privileges.

Impact & Exploitation

  • Arbitrary Code Execution: Malicious executable runs with high privileges.
  • Privilege Escalation: Gain SYSTEM or Administrator access.
  • Persistence: If service restarts, payload re-executes.
Code Example: Identifying Unquoted Paths
wmic service get name,displayname,pathname,startmode | findstr /i "auto" | findstr /i /v "c:\windows\\" | findstr /i /v """
This command identifies services with automatic startup, not in the Windows directory, and without quoted paths.
Key Takeaway

Unquoted service paths allow Windows to execute malicious code placed in intermediate path segments with elevated service privileges.

screens.title: Weak Service Permissions
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond unquoted paths, another significant service misconfiguration involves weak service permissions. Services, as we know, often run with high privileges. If a low-privileged user has write permissions to a service's executable file itself, or the ability to modify the service's configuration, they can directly replace the legitimate executable with their own malicious payload. Alternatively, they could reconfigure the service to point to a different, attacker-controlled binary. Imagine a scenario where the 'Everyone' group has 'Modify' or 'Full Control' permissions on a critical service's executable. An attacker could simply swap out the original program with a reverse shell or a user-creation script. When the service restarts, the malicious code executes with the service's privileges, which could be LocalSystem. Tools like icacls are essential for checking these file system permissions, while sc qc can query service configurations. This vulnerability highlights the importance of proper access control on system binaries and service settings, as insecure permissions can provide a direct avenue for privilege escalation. Weak Service Permissions means weak permissions on service executables or configurations allow low-privileged users to replace or reconfigure services for elevated code execution.. In practical terms, gaining control by modifying service executables or configurations.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5›Chapter 5.3›Weak Service Permissions
Vulnerability Deep Dive

Weak Service Permissions

Gaining control by modifying service executables or configurations.

Exploitation Scenarios

  • Executable Replacement: Low-priv user has write access to the service's .exe.
  • Service Reconfiguration: Low-priv user can modify service binary path (e.g., via sc config).
  • DLL Hijacking: If service loads a DLL from a writable path, replace it with malicious DLL.

Common Weak Permissions

  • (M) - Modify: Allows changing the file.
  • (F) - Full control: Complete control over the file.
  • Often found for BUILTIN\Users or Everyone groups.
Code Example: Checking Permissions
icacls "C:\Program Files\Vulnerable Service\vulnerable.exe"
This command displays the Access Control List (ACL) for the specified service executable. Look for 'M' or 'F' for low-privileged groups.
Key Takeaway

Weak permissions on service executables or configurations allow low-privileged users to replace or reconfigure services for elevated code execution.

screens.title: Insecure Scheduled Tasks
screens.narratorSegment: Just like cron jobs on Linux, Windows has scheduled tasks that automate the execution of programs or scripts at specific times or intervals. These tasks can be configured to run with elevated privileges, such as SYSTEM or an administrator account, to perform necessary system maintenance or operations. The vulnerability arises when a low-privileged user can modify the executable or script that a scheduled task is configured to run. If you can replace the legitimate program with your own malicious code, or even inject code into an existing script, your payload will then execute with the elevated privileges of the scheduled task. Enumerating these tasks using commands like schtasks /query /fo LIST /v is crucial. This command provides detailed information, including the user context under which the task runs and the path to the executable. Once identified, checking the permissions on those executables becomes the next logical step. If you find a task running as SYSTEM and you have write access to its associated binary, you have a clear path to privilege escalation. This technique exploits the trust placed in automated processes.

keyIdea.title: Automating Elevated Execution
keyIdea.text: Insecure scheduled tasks allow attackers to inject malicious code into programs run by high-privileged tasks, leading to privilege escalation.

content.html:
Module 5›Chapter 5.3›Insecure Scheduled Tasks
Exploitation Vector

Insecure Scheduled Tasks

Leveraging automated tasks for elevated code execution.

How Scheduled Tasks Work

  • Automate program/script execution at specific times or events.
  • Can run with elevated privileges (e.g., SYSTEM, Administrator).
  • Configuration stored in XML files or registry.

Exploiting Insecure Tasks

  • Modify Executable: Replace the legitimate program with a malicious one.
  • Inject Code: Modify a script run by the task to include your payload.
  • Requires write permissions on the task's executable or script.
Code Example: Enumerating Scheduled Tasks
schtasks /query /fo LIST /v
This command lists all scheduled tasks with verbose details, including the 'Run As' user and the 'Task Command' (executable path).
Key Takeaway

Insecure scheduled tasks allow attackers to inject malicious code into programs run by high-privileged tasks, leading to privilege escalation.

screens.title: AlwaysInstallElevated Policy
screens.narratorSegment: The AlwaysInstallElevated policy is a less common but incredibly effective privilege escalation technique. When this specific registry setting is enabled, it allows any user, regardless of their current privilege level, to install Windows Installer (. msi) packages with SYSTEM privileges. This policy essentially tells Windows to always perform installations with the highest possible privileges, bypassing standard user access controls. An attacker can exploit this by crafting a malicious. msi package. This package could be designed to execute a command, drop a backdoor, or create a new administrator account. Once the malicious. msi is created, the attacker simply installs it, and their payload executes with SYSTEM access. To check if this vulnerability exists, you need to query two specific registry keys: one in HKCU (current user) and one in HKLM (local machine). If AlwaysInstallElevated is set to 1 in both locations, the system is vulnerable. This policy, while intended to simplify software deployment in some enterprise settings, creates a significant security loophole if misconfigured. AlwaysInstallElevated Policy means when alwaysinstallelevated is enabled, any user can install malicious msi packages with system privileges, bypassing normal security checks.. In practical terms, installing malicious msi packages with system privileges.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5›Chapter 5.3›AlwaysInstallElevated Policy
Policy Exploitation

AlwaysInstallElevated Policy

Installing malicious MSI packages with SYSTEM privileges.

What it is

  • A Windows registry setting.
  • When enabled, allows any user to install .msi packages with SYSTEM privileges.
  • Bypasses standard user access controls for installations.

Exploitation Steps

  • Craft a malicious .msi package (e.g., using msfvenom).
  • The .msi executes a command or drops a backdoor.
  • Install the malicious .msi to gain SYSTEM access.
Code Example: Checking Registry Keys
reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevatedreg query HKCU\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated
Check if 'AlwaysInstallElevated' is set to '1' in both HKLM and HKCU paths.
Key Takeaway

When AlwaysInstallElevated is enabled, any user can install malicious MSI packages with SYSTEM privileges, bypassing normal security checks.

screens.title: Stored Credentials: A Goldmine for Attackers
screens.narratorSegment: Stored credentials are an absolute goldmine for privilege escalation and lateral movement within a network. Windows systems frequently store various forms of authentication data, including plaintext passwords, NTLM hashes, and Kerberos tickets, in memory or within the Security Account Manager, or SAM, database. These credentials represent the keys to other systems and higher privileges. If an attacker can extract these, they can often gain access to other user accounts, including administrative ones, without needing to crack passwords. This is where Mimikatz comes into play. Mimikatz is the quintessential tool for extracting these sensitive credentials. It's a powerful post-exploitation utility specifically designed to interact with the Windows Local Security Authority Subsystem Service, or LSASS, process, which handles security policies and user authentication. While Mimikatz typically requires SYSTEM privileges to access the most sensitive memory regions, some versions can operate with administrator privileges. Understanding how and where Windows stores credentials is the first step to effectively using tools like Mimikatz to uncover them. In practical terms, uncovering sensitive authentication data from windows memory.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: PowerSploit's PowerUp.ps1 Module
screens.narratorSegment: Another powerful framework for Windows privilege escalation is PowerSploit, and specifically its PowerUp. ps1 module. PowerSploit is a collection of PowerShell scripts designed for offensive security, and PowerUp is dedicated to identifying and exploiting many Windows privilege escalation vectors. Unlike WinPEAS, which is a standalone script, PowerUp is a PowerShell module that can be loaded and executed directly within a PowerShell session. It includes functions like Get-ServiceUnquotedPath to find unquoted service paths or Invoke-BypassUAC to bypass User Account Control. The most commonly used function for initial enumeration is Invoke-AllChecks, which, as its name suggests, runs a battery of checks to identify various vulnerabilities. Before running PowerUp, you might need to bypass the PowerShell execution policy, typically using Set-ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Scope Process -Force. PowerUp's integration with PowerShell makes it highly flexible and often less prone to immediate detection than standalone executables, though it still requires careful handling. It’s an essential tool for any penetration tester operating in a PowerShell-rich Windows environment. screens.title: Interpreting Results and Manual Verification
screens.narratorSegment: While automated tools like WinPEAS and PowerSploit are incredibly efficient for enumerating potential privilege escalation vectors, a common mistake is not fully understanding their output. These tools can generate a lot of information, and not every 'finding' is immediately exploitable or even a true vulnerability in a given context. It's crucial to interpret the findings critically and, where possible, verify them manually. For example, if a tool flags an unquoted service path, you should manually confirm the service's permissions and whether you can write to the intermediate path. Prioritization is also key: focus on vulnerabilities that offer the most direct and reliable path to SYSTEM or administrative privileges. Some vulnerabilities might be harder to exploit or require specific conditions that aren't met. Your expertise as a penetration tester in interpreting these results and safely exploiting vulnerabilities remains paramount. Automated tools are powerful assistants, but they don't replace human judgment and a deep understanding of the underlying techniques. Always validate and prioritize to ensure your efforts are effective and efficient. fullNarratorScript:
Welcome to Chapter 5.3, focusing on Windows Privilege Escalation Techniques. In the world of penetration testing, gaining initial access to a system is just the first step. Often, you'll find yourself with limited user privileges, which isn't enough to achieve your objectives. This chapter is all about understanding how to elevate those privileges on Windows systems, moving from a low-level user to a powerful administrator or even NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM. We'll explore the unique challenges and opportunities that Windows environments present, from common misconfigurations in services and scheduled tasks to leveraging specific policies and extracting sensitive credentials. By the end of this chapter, you'll have a robust toolkit and a methodical approach to effectively escalate privileges, a critical skill for any professional penetration tester. Get ready to dive deep into the intricacies of Windows security and learn how to exploit its weaknesses to your advantage.

In this first set of learning objectives, we'll lay the groundwork for understanding Windows privilege escalation. First, you will learn to identify common misconfigurations and vulnerabilities inherent in Windows systems that frequently enable privilege escalation. This involves recognizing patterns and specific settings that attackers often target. Next, we'll focus on exploiting service misconfigurations, a prevalent vector. You'll gain practical skills in leveraging issues like unquoted service paths and weak service permissions to execute your own code with elevated privileges. Finally, we'll explore how to leverage insecure scheduled tasks and the AlwaysInstallElevated policy, two distinct yet powerful methods for gaining higher access. These foundational skills are crucial for building a comprehensive understanding of Windows exploitation and will prepare you for more advanced techniques. Learning Objectives means master the core techniques for identifying and exploiting windows misconfigurations and policies to achieve elevated privileges.. In practical terms, what you'll achieve in this chapter. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Building upon our foundational knowledge, this second set of objectives will equip you with advanced tools and methodologies. You will learn how to extract credentials from memory using powerful tools like Mimikatz. This critical skill allows you to uncover plaintext passwords, hashes, and Kerberos tickets, which are invaluable for further system compromise and lateral movement. We'll then move on to utilizing automated tools such as WinPEAS and PowerSploit for comprehensive privilege escalation enumeration on Windows. These tools significantly streamline the discovery process, helping you quickly identify potential vulnerabilities. Finally, you'll learn to apply a methodical approach to privilege escalation, understanding how to interpret tool output, verify findings manually, and prioritize the most effective exploitation paths. This holistic understanding will enable you to execute successful and efficient privilege escalation attacks in real-world scenarios.

When you first gain access to a Windows system, you'll often find yourself operating with low-level user privileges. This means you can't install software, modify critical system files, or access sensitive data. The primary goal of Windows privilege escalation is to elevate these limited privileges, typically aiming for NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM or a local administrator account. Think of NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM as the Windows equivalent of 'root' on a Linux system – it grants ultimate control. Windows environments present a unique set of challenges and opportunities compared to Linux, largely due to its distinct architecture, service management, and security model. For instance, Windows relies heavily on the registry for configuration and has a different approach to user and group permissions. Understanding these fundamental differences is absolutely key to successfully identifying and exploiting vulnerabilities. Without elevated privileges, your ability to further compromise a system or achieve your objectives is severely limited, making this a crucial phase in any penetration test. Understanding Windows Privilege Escalation means privilege escalation aims to gain higher access on windows, moving from a low-privileged user to full system control.. In practical terms, elevating access from low-level user to system.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

One of the most common and often easily exploitable vulnerabilities on Windows involves service misconfigurations, specifically unquoted service paths. Windows services are programs that run in the background, often with elevated privileges like LocalSystem. When a service's executable path contains spaces, such as 'C:\Program Files\My Application\service. exe', but isn't enclosed in quotation marks, Windows can misinterpret the path. Instead of executing the full path, the operating system might sequentially try to execute each component of the path before the next space. For example, it might first attempt to run 'C:\Program. exe', then 'C:\Program Files\My. exe', and so on. If a low-privileged user can write to any of these intermediate paths, they can place a malicious executable there. When the legitimate service starts or restarts, Windows will inadvertently execute the attacker's payload with the service's high privileges. This is a powerful technique because it leverages a fundamental parsing error in how Windows handles file paths. Identifying these services is a critical first step in exploiting this vulnerability. Unquoted Service Paths means unquoted service paths allow windows to execute malicious code placed in intermediate path segments with elevated service privileges.. In practical terms, exploiting windows' path interpretation for privilege escalation.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Beyond unquoted paths, another significant service misconfiguration involves weak service permissions. Services, as we know, often run with high privileges. If a low-privileged user has write permissions to a service's executable file itself, or the ability to modify the service's configuration, they can directly replace the legitimate executable with their own malicious payload. Alternatively, they could reconfigure the service to point to a different, attacker-controlled binary. Imagine a scenario where the 'Everyone' group has 'Modify' or 'Full Control' permissions on a critical service's executable. An attacker could simply swap out the original program with a reverse shell or a user-creation script. When the service restarts, the malicious code executes with the service's privileges, which could be LocalSystem. Tools like icacls are essential for checking these file system permissions, while sc qc can query service configurations. This vulnerability highlights the importance of proper access control on system binaries and service settings, as insecure permissions can provide a direct avenue for privilege escalation. Weak Service Permissions means weak permissions on service executables or configurations allow low-privileged users to replace or reconfigure services for elevated code execution.. In practical terms, gaining control by modifying service executables or configurations.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Just like cron jobs on Linux, Windows has scheduled tasks that automate the execution of programs or scripts at specific times or intervals. These tasks can be configured to run with elevated privileges, such as SYSTEM or an administrator account, to perform necessary system maintenance or operations. The vulnerability arises when a low-privileged user can modify the executable or script that a scheduled task is configured to run. If you can replace the legitimate program with your own malicious code, or even inject code into an existing script, your payload will then execute with the elevated privileges of the scheduled task. Enumerating these tasks using commands like schtasks /query /fo LIST /v is crucial. This command provides detailed information, including the user context under which the task runs and the path to the executable. Once identified, checking the permissions on those executables becomes the next logical step. If you find a task running as SYSTEM and you have write access to its associated binary, you have a clear path to privilege escalation. This technique exploits the trust placed in automated processes.

The AlwaysInstallElevated policy is a less common but incredibly effective privilege escalation technique. When this specific registry setting is enabled, it allows any user, regardless of their current privilege level, to install Windows Installer (. msi) packages with SYSTEM privileges. This policy essentially tells Windows to always perform installations with the highest possible privileges, bypassing standard user access controls. An attacker can exploit this by crafting a malicious. msi package. This package could be designed to execute a command, drop a backdoor, or create a new administrator account. Once the malicious. msi is created, the attacker simply installs it, and their payload executes with SYSTEM access. Let's recap some of the essential concepts we've covered in Windows privilege escalation. First, NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM represents the highest privilege level on a Windows operating system, akin to the 'root' user in Linux. Achieving this level of access is often the ultimate goal of privilege escalation. Next, we discussed Service Misconfiguration, which refers to vulnerabilities arising from improperly configured Windows services. These often relate to how their executable paths are defined or the permissions set on their files. Finally, a specific type of service misconfiguration is the Unquoted Service Path. This vulnerability occurs when a service's executable path contains spaces but isn't enclosed in quotes, potentially allowing an attacker to execute arbitrary code with elevated privileges by placing a malicious file in an intermediate path. Understanding these foundational terms is crucial for grasping the mechanics of Windows exploitation.

Continuing our review, let's look at more advanced concepts in Windows privilege escalation. Weak Service Permissions are insecure permissions on a service's executable or its configuration, allowing a low-privileged user to modify or replace the service's binary, leading to elevated code execution. This directly compromises the integrity of the service. Then, we explored the AlwaysInstallElevated policy. When this Windows policy is enabled, it allows any user to install Windows Installer, or. msi, packages with SYSTEM privileges, creating a significant loophole for attackers to gain full control. Lastly, Mimikatz is a powerful post-exploitation tool for Windows. It's specifically designed to extract plaintext passwords, NTLM hashes, PINs, and Kerberos tickets directly from memory. Mimikatz is an indispensable tool for credential harvesting, which can then be used for further privilege escalation or lateral movement within a network. These concepts represent potent attack vectors that you'll encounter in real-world penetration tests.
